what_its_for: This medicine helps control high phosphorus levels in your blood. It is used in adults who are on dialysis (either hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) for kidney disease. High phosphorus can harm your bones, heart, and blood vessels, so keeping it under control is very important.
how_to_take: Chew these tablets completely — do not swallow them whole. Take them with meals or snacks. Chewing the tablets well before swallowing helps the medicine work properly. The tablets may cause some discoloration of your stools (they may appear dark or black), which is normal and not harmful. Try to take this medicine at the same meals every day to keep a steady routine.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 3 chewable tablets per day, spread out across your main meals (for example, 1 tablet with each of 3 meals). Your doctor will adjust your dose based on your blood phosphorus levels, typically checking them every 2 to 4 weeks. The maximum recommended dose is 6 tablets per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose with your next meal. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Just continue with your regular schedule.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in its original container and keep the container tightly closed. Keep it away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other medicines within 1 to 2 hours of taking sucroferric oxyhydroxide, as it may affect how well other medicines are absorbed into your body. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements. Avoid eating high-phosphorus foods such as dairy products, nuts, seeds, processed foods, and dark colas, as diet is also an important part of managing your phosphorus levels.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you experience: severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that does not go away; difficulty swallowing or chewing the tablets; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; unusual or severe constipation; or if you feel your phosphorus is not being controlled. Also tell your doctor about all medicines and supplements you take, including over-the-counter products.
when_it_works: Your doctor will check your blood phosphorus levels regularly, usually every 2 to 4 weeks, to see how well the medicine is working. You may not feel any different right away, but lowering your phosphorus levels over time helps protect your bones, heart, and blood vessels. It is important to keep taking this medicine and following your diet plan even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you have iron overload conditions such as hemochromatosis, or if you have had stomach or bowel surgery, as this medicine may not be right for you. This medicine is not approved for use in children. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using this medicine, as its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully established. Older adults can generally take this medicine safely, but should be monitored regularly by their healthcare team.
